The card divides the 2 shared neighbors by the 5 distinct neighbors: Jaccard similarity 0.4." width="100%"} The Jaccard index is a classic set similarity measure: `Jaccard(A, B) = |neighbors(A) ∩ neighbors(B)| / |neighbors(A) ∪ neighbors(B)|` Range: `[0, 1]` where `0` means no common neighbors and `1` means identical neighborhoods (or same node). More conservative than Dice coefficient (always ≤ Dice score). Self-similarity is always `1.0`, and two nodes that both have no neighbors score `0.0`. Two nodes get a high score when most of the nodes they touch are shared, regardless of whether they are adjacent to each other. Because the score is normalized by the size of the combined neighborhood, it is not inflated for high-degree nodes the way a raw common-neighbor count is. In an undirected graph the neighborhood is every adjacent node. In a directed graph only out-neighbors (edge targets) are compared, so nodes that point to the same targets are similar while nodes that are only pointed *to* by the same sources score `0.0`. Every pair of nodes is scored, so both time and the size of the returned dictionary grow quadratically with the number of nodes. On large graphs, prefer `pairwise_similarity()` with an explicit `nodes=` list to score only the nodes of interest. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, dict[int, float]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Nested dictionary mapping node IDs to dictionaries of similarity scores. Format: `{node1_id: {node2_id: similarity_score}}`. Every node appears as an outer key and every inner dictionary contains all nodes (including the node itself). ::: ## Common Use Cases {.doc-common-use-cases} - document similarity (bag-of-words) - user similarity (common items/friends) - biological networks (protein interactions) ## Examples {.doc-examples} Every leaf of this star shares the hub as its only neighbor, so any two leaves have identical neighborhoods and a Jaccard similarity of `1.0`: ::: {#4b51dd79 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["hub", "A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("hub", "A"), ("hub", "B"), ("hub", "C")]) ) sim = graph.jaccard_similarity() a_id = graph.get_id_from_label("A") b_id = graph.get_id_from_label("B") sim[a_id][b_id] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 1.0 ``` ::: ::: The hub, on the other hand, shares no neighbors with any leaf (its neighbors are the leaves themselves), so its similarity to each of them is `0.0`. Converting the IDs to labels makes the hub's row easy to read: ::: {#1d6a2b05 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} hub_id = graph.get_id_from_label("hub") {graph.get_label_from_id(nid): s for nid, s in sim[hub_id].items()} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {'B': 0.0, 'hub': 1.0, 'C': 0.0, 'A': 0.0} ``` ::: ::: With partial overlap the score falls between the extremes. "P" and "Q" share two of the four distinct nodes they connect to, giving `2 / 4 = 0.5`: ::: {#9c623687 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_nodes(["P", "Q", "W", "X", "Y", "Z"]) graph.add_edges([("P", "W"), ("P", "X"), ("P", "Y"), ("Q", "X"), ("Q", "Y"), ("Q", "Z")]) sim = graph.jaccard_similarity() sim[graph.get_id_from_label("P")][graph.get_id_from_label("Q")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 0.5 ``` ::: :::
